debris.notes: A curved sheet of blackened skin off a booster fairing, light enough to tether without thinking and common enough to be the first thing most players ever latch.
A crumpled ball of multi-layer foil that barely registers on the tether, the cheapest thing in the sky and the safest filler for a last slot.
Separation hardware fused into a knot of studs and collars, dense for its size and the closest thing the low sky has to honest metal.
A folded length of lattice strut that swings wide on every turn, the piece that teaches a new player what a towed load actually feels like.
Ground-support steel that rode up with something and never came down, the heaviest routine haul in the cheap band.
A springy monopole that glints as it tumbles, almost weightless on the line but never crushable, so it costs full uncrushed slots the whole way home.
Laminated capsule glass with a star fracture through it, the suborbital band's one real prize and the first lesson in landing gently.
Half a payload fairing the size of a garage door; rejects the hand magnet outright and waits for the crane cable, so it sits in the sky as a preview of a tool the shipping slice does not have.
A sealed drum of bearing steel and copper, the bread-and-butter satellite wreckage of the low band and heavy enough that the trip home has to be planned.
A ruptured titanium sphere still wearing its mounting collar, the heaviest hand-tetherable piece a mid-game player will routinely try to drag.
A boxed rack of flight computers, solid enough to shrug off a mediocre landing and worth more than anything the suborbital band offers.
Three rate gyros still bolted to their machined mount, dense for one slot and the efficient pick when the hold is nearly full.
Four attitude jets on a common manifold, compact and forgiving, the low band's answer to the hull panel.
A wing of cells with half its panes starred; light for its bulk but never crushable, so it eats four slots and doubles every point of heat and landing damage.
A baffled optical head with the lens still clean, small and precious and the cheapest way for the player to learn what fragile costs on the way down.
A parabolic mesh reflector that catches the sun on a slow cycle from half a screen away, spawning off the clumps and above its band so reaching it is a real burn.
The gutted spaceframe of a comsat, crane-cable only and heavy enough on its own to change the reentry profile; unreachable in the shipping slice by design.
The dense structural heart of a constellation satellite, the high band's staple and by itself a third of what a starting hold can carry.
A shielded block off a dead nuclear power unit, the single heaviest hand-tetherable piece in the game and a deliberate test of whether the player's chute can still hold five metres a second.
A turbopump and its cold plumbing welded into one lump, solid enough to survive a rough entry when the rest of the haul will not.
A wrapped cylinder of science hardware, one slot crushed and dense with the good metals, the high band's efficiency pick.
A thermoelectric generator casing built to survive reentry on its own, absurdly heavy for one slot and the strongest argument for a Parachute upgrade.
A mirror and its invar frame, heavy and uncrushable at once, so a single one occupies four slots and doubles its own damage the whole way down.
A pointing head with its optics intact, dense for a small piece and fragile with it, so latch jerk at high closing speed is the real risk rather than the tow.

A rigid high-gain antenna off something that was never meant to come back, glinting on its own fast orbit well off the clumps; the whole skill chain from crossing to touchdown pays out on this one piece.
A whole geostationary bird minus its arrays, crane-cable only and heavier than the empty ship; it is the rehearsal object for Mr. Armstrong's satellite and is deferred with the class it belongs to.

design_notes: Mean mass rises 36.19 -> 72.33 -> 167.33 kg, roughly 2x per band and 4.6x from suborbital to high; excluding the crane-only oversized piece from each band the same climb is 15.6 -> 39.0 -> 114.5 kg, about 7.3x, so the mass gradient is carried by the ordinary hand-tetherable pieces and not by the one outlier per band.

The Researcher's finding that entry speed only spans 151-164 m/s across all three bands means altitude cannot produce the band difficulty curve. This catalog puts that load on mass instead, which is the lever GDD 4.5 risk 2 already names: a full high-band hold is several times the tonnage of a full suborbital one under the same chute and the same shield, so deceleration authority falls and integrated heat rises exactly as the haul gets good.

Fragile spawn weight is 6/60 = 0.100 in suborbital, 8/46 = 0.174 in low and 10/40 = 0.250 in high, computed as the weighted share rather than the piece-count share. By count the three bands are 2/8, 3/9 and 3/9, which would read as 0.25 everywhere - the weights are what hold the 1-in-10 to 1-in-4 gradient the GDD asks for.

Fragile pieces get low spawn weights within their band and are deliberately not the lightest things in it: cracked_viewport_pane, dish_reflector, optical_bench and deep_space_dish all cost full uncrushed slots forever and all take double heat and landing damage, so a fragile-heavy run is a genuinely worse ride home rather than free money.

Every size class and the fragile flag appear in both shipping-slice bands, so a player who never leaves suborbital and low still meets small, medium, oversized-that-rejects-the-hand-magnet, and fragile. The oversized pieces are one per band and exist to make the catalog complete; all three are unreachable without the crane magnet the semester scope cuts.

Medium is not hoarded in the top band - suborbital carries 2 mediums, low 5 and high 5 - so the skew toward medium is a shift in spawn weight and mass, not a class the player only meets after the slice ends. High-band smalls (rtg_capsule at 88 kg, sensor_gimbal_head at 60 kg) are heavier than most low-band mediums, which is how the band reads as dense rather than merely bulky.

Slot economics stay non-degenerate at every band: at 6 starting slots and roughly 500 kg of usable capacity, one crushed high-band medium is about a third of the hold, one crushed high-band small is about a sixth, and an uncrushed fragile medium is two thirds of it. No piece is strictly dominant because the best mass-per-slot pieces (gold_foil_instrument_can, gyro_cluster) are the ones the Economy Balancer can price below the fragile pieces that cost four slots to bring home.
